But like the slave revolts of earlier periods, this uprising had little chance of success.

The rebels did not even have the weapons they needed to defend themselves. Nor did they receive support from other oppressed social groups, such as poor peasants, artisans, and other exploited people.
Slavery still had an accepted place in the social order, and Islam itself recognized it. Islam even forbade slaves from leaving the ownership of their “masters” without those masters’ consent.
At the same time, Islam did introduce laws that required slave owners, in certain cases, to free some of their slaves as an act of atonement for particular sins.
The slave revolt in Damascus therefore failed, and ʿAbd al-Malik’s army crushed it.
Yet the commander of that army ordered his soldiers not to kill the rebel slaves, out of respect for the property rights of their “masters”!.
ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān and al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik became known for major administrative and civil reforms in the history of the Umayyad state.

Among these were the minting of Arab coinage, the first measure of its kind; the Arabization of the state registers for the first time; an attempt to separate the powers of the different administrative departments so that each could be kept under better control; and the expansion of the conquests across large parts of Asia and Africa, and even into Europe.

These conquests expanded the Arab state and extended Arab and Islamic rule over many different countries and peoples. Their entry into Arab political history had a clear effect on Arab culture, making it more varied and enriching it.
But the conquests also had negative effects on economic, administrative, and social policy.
First, expansion weakened the central power of the state.

As conquest spread, the governor of each province began to behave almost like an independent ruler, or like the head of a state within the state. He might send only part of his tax revenue to the central caliphal government and keep the rest for himself.
The same was true of the spoils of conquest. He would send only one fifth to the central government and keep the remaining four fifths to use as he pleased.
Second, continued expansion required more spending on armies, on the defense of conquered lands, and on the administration of public affairs.
A state ruled by representatives of a wealthy class that exploits the majority naturally places most of its costs on that same majority.

This is exactly what began to happen more and more under the Umayyad state from this period onward, until the dynasty eventually collapsed under the pressure of social uprisings as well as political conflicts that had become deeply entangled with them.
One example was the uprising that took place in the lands of the Turks in Central Asia in 73 AH.
The works of Arab historians are full of accounts of what happened there during that year and the years that followed.

These accounts make it clear that Umayyad financial policy was the main cause of the resentment that built up and intensified until it became a series of armed uprisings that nearly destroyed Umayyad authority in the Turkic lands.
Many of the local people had converted to Islam.
But the Umayyad authorities continued to collect the jizya from them even after their conversion, and then added new taxes on top of it.
The Turkic kings, led by the “Great Khagan,” used the anger of the common people as an opportunity to recover their own power. They fought long and exhausting wars against the Umayyad state.

Some Arabs in the region who followed the movement known as the Murjiʾa sided with the discontented population. They supported the people’s demand that the Umayyad authorities reduce their tax burden and the harshness of tax collection.
We have presented this historical picture in some detail so that we can now see more clearly how political events and social conditions gave rise to intellectual movements.

Intellectual activity became so deeply mixed with political and social conflict that it is difficult to find any intellectual movement that appeared after the rise of Umayyad rule without finding roots in those events and conditions.
In some cases, particular parts of an intellectual movement were directly connected with a particular side of a political or social struggle.
We will point out these connections when we reach them.
B — The Shiʿa: A Position and a “Theory”
We cannot completely separate a political or intellectual position from the theory behind it.
A position on any question, opinion, or movement is hardly worth serious attention unless it rests on some kind of theoretical thought or basic principle.
The reverse is also true. To accept a particular theory about a question is itself a position. Otherwise, the theory becomes a pure abstraction hanging in empty space.
So there is a dialectical relationship between position and theory. That relationship makes it impossible to separate them completely.
But for the sake of study and explanation, we need to make a formal distinction between them here.
With that in mind, we can say that Shiʿism, as a position within Islam, arose with the question of the caliphate immediately after the death of the Prophet.
That position then developed and interacted with events in Arab-Islamic life.
From it came a range of political and intellectual positions, including theological and philosophical ones. These eventually formed many different Shiʿi schools and sects.
Some changed into positions very different from where they had begun.
Others grew stronger, developed a wider base, and still continue today with their original foundations largely intact.

However much the Shiʿi groups differed throughout history in their principles, interpretations, and degree of attachment to the basic teachings of Islam, most of them shared one thing: their position toward the person of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

That position often became, deliberately or otherwise, directly or indirectly, an expression of a political or class position toward one ruler or another under the Islamic caliphates, whether Umayyad, Abbasid, or something else.
Most often, this political or class position took the form of opposition.
And that opposition was often marked by bloodshed and violence: sometimes through battles and armed uprisings, and sometimes through political persecution so severe that it became outright massacre.
We have already discussed one of the earliest Shiʿi uprisings against the Umayyads.

Shiʿi political opposition to ruling governments continued through most of the Abbasid period. Political persecution of the Shiʿa also continued through different stages of Arab-Islamic political history, down to the end of the Turkish Ottoman caliphate in the early twentieth century.

The Shiʿi position shifted from opposition to support only during periods when Shiʿi rulers came to power, such as the Buyid state in Iran, the emirate of Sayf al-Dawla al-Ḥamdānī in Aleppo during the fourth century AH—the tenth century CE—and the Fatimid state in North Africa and Egypt during that same century.
There were also occasional periods of accommodation between Shiʿi groups and particular caliphs, such as the Abbasid caliph al-Maʾmūn.
Here we can see another important feature of Shiʿi history.
Political opposition often took on a social character as well.

In other words, the opposition was not always directed mainly at the form of government or at the individual rulers themselves. At a deeper level, it was often opposition to the way those rulers treated weak and oppressed social classes and groups.
It is quite possible that this had something to do with the position of ordinary Shiʿis themselves.

Many of them suffered social oppression alongside political persecution because they were themselves an organic part of the same social classes and groups that were being oppressed by the ruling classes.
It is difficult to give one complete and absolute definition of Shiʿi theory.

After the death of the fourth imam, ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, known as Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn—the son who survived the massacre at Karbala in which his father al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī was killed—the Shiʿa began to divide into different groups.
The first was the Imāmiyya, the followers of Imam Muḥammad al-Bāqir, son of Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn.
The second was the Zaydiyya, the followers of Zayd ibn ʿAlī Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn.
The third was the Kaysāniyya, the followers of Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, who was a direct son of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and was known by the name of his mother, al-Ḥanafiyya.
As the first signs of theological and philosophical thought began to appear, Shiʿi groups continued to divide and develop.
This happened because new ideas kept entering Shiʿi theory from the wider intellectual movement that was beginning to take shape.
At first, this intellectual movement centered on the problem of divine decree, human responsibility for human actions, and the relationship between human action and divine action.
It was also closely connected with the political struggle over the caliphate, and especially with opposition to the Umayyad caliphate.
Later, these questions became more clearly developed as the growing movement of theological and philosophical thought gathered strength.
So it may be difficult to give one complete definition of Shiʿi theory.
But it is not difficult to identify its earliest foundations—the basic idea from which the many different Shiʿi religious and intellectual theories later developed.

Despite the differences between their sects and schools, Shiʿis begin from the belief that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib was the Muslim with the first and strongest right to political authority after the Prophet.
They believe that this authority is a divine right, not something for people themselves to decide by choosing whoever they believe is best suited to lead.
Only God, they argue, knows where the true interests of human beings lie and what will bring them well-being in this world and the next.
For this reason, the Shiʿa regarded the imamate as one of the fundamental pillars of Islam—that is, as one of the basic principles of Islamic belief.
This is the firm foundation of Shiʿi theory, whatever differences later developed over the form and character of this authority, whether spiritual or political.
Beyond this point, Shiʿi groups differ greatly.
There are moderate Shiʿis, and there are those who went to extremes in the kind of authority they gave to the person of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.
The latter are known in Islamic history as the ghulāt, the extremists, because they pushed their beliefs so far that some of them gave divine qualities to ʿAlī himself.
Moderate Shiʿis and Sunnis agree that these extremist groups fall outside the basic principles of Islamic belief.
Historians, however, often use the name “Shiʿa” for any group whose theory is fundamentally connected with the person of ʿAlī.
The Imāmiyya, the Twelvers, and the Zaydiyya reject this use of the term and deny that the extremist groups should be counted as Shiʿi.

Their rejection of extremism rests, first, on their Islamic belief in the absolute oneness of God: that God has no body and that nothing in creation is like Him. It also rests on their belief in Muḥammad’s prophethood, and in resurrection and life in the world to come.
Second, they point to a statement attributed to Imam ʿAlī in one of his sermons:

“Two kinds of people will be destroyed because of me: one who loves me so excessively that his love takes him away from the truth, and one who hates me so excessively that his hatred takes him away from the truth. The best position is the middle way, so hold to it.”
Shiʿi sources also report the statement in another form:
“Two kinds of people are destroyed because of me: one who loves me to excess, and one who hates me with bitterness.”
The fourth Shiʿi imam, ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn, expressed the same idea:
“People, love us with the love that Islam teaches. Your love has kept growing until it has become a source of shame for us.”
3 — The Theory of the Moderate Shiʿa
The full theory of the moderate Shiʿi groups rests, first, on the basic principles of Islamic belief that we have just discussed.
Second, it rests on the claim that the right to the caliphate after the Prophet belonged directly to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, and then successively to his descendants.

God chooses for it whoever He wishes from among those who are greatest in knowledge, character, and religion. Because God makes this choice, He must also identify the person He has chosen through the words of His Prophet Muḥammad.
To prove that ʿAlī himself was the person chosen by God, the Shiʿa use two kinds of argument.
